results.title: Why Your Hibiscus Leaves are Turning Yellow (3 FIXES!)
results.description:
#hibiscuscare #yellowleaves #gudhal
Why Your Hibiscus Leaves are Turning Yellow (3 FIXES!) | Garden Decoded

🌿 If your hibiscus has yellow leaves with green veins still visible — especially on new growth — your soil pH is almost certainly the culprit. In this video I explain exactly what is happening inside your soil at the chemical level, how to test for it in under 5 minutes at home, and three proven methods to fix it permanently.

🌿 Even with proper watering and feeding, yellow leaves on your hibiscus plant can signal a deeper issue: soil pH. This video explains how soil pH can block nutrient absorption, causing your hibiscus plant to stay sick. We'll show you how to conduct accurate soil testing to determine your soil's pH and provide practical gardening tips on using sulfur as a soil amendment to bring your plant back to health. Give your hibiscus the care it deserves!

You can fertilise a hibiscus every week and still watch it go yellow — because when pH is wrong, iron locks into an insoluble form that roots cannot absorb no matter how much you feed. I explain the mechanism behind every fix so you understand not just what to do but why it works.

You've been watching those hibiscus buds form for weeks — and now they're falling off before they even have a chance to open. Hibiscus bud drop is one of the most frustrating plant problems because it happens just when you're about to see the payoff. But it's almost never random. Your plant is trying to tell you something. Every brown tip, every yellow leaf, every spot and curl is a specific message — and once you know how to read them, you'll never misdiagnose a sick plant again.
This video covers every common houseplant leaf problem — what causes brown tips, why leaves turn yellow, what leaf curling means, and how to identify and fix every symptom your plant shows. 2:51 Leaves curling inward — underwatering and heat stress
3:39 Leaves curling downward — overfertilisation and excess nitrogen
4:32 Dark brown or black spots with yellow halo — fungal infection

6:58 White powdery coating on leaves — powdery mildew treatment
7:40 Silvery or bronze sheen on leaves — thrips damage
8:24 Pale washed-out bleached leaves — too much direct sunlight
9:06 Dark almost black leaves — not enough light

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

→ Why brown tips on houseplants almost never mean disease — and what they actually mean

───────────────────────────────────────────
QUICK LEAF SYMPTOM REFERENCE — save this
───────────────────────────────────────────
Brown crispy tips                    → Low humidity, dry air, or underwatering
Yellow leaves — lower only           → Normal aging if slow and gradual
Yellow leaves — all over the plant   → Overwatering or root oxygen loss
Leaves curling inward                → Underwatering or heat stress
Leaves curling downward              → Overfertilisation or excess nitrogen
Dark spots with yellow halo          → Fungal infection
Tiny pale dots, stippling pattern    → Spider mites
Soft translucent mushy patches       → Cold damage
White powdery coating                → Powdery mildew
Silvery or bronze sheen              → Thrips damage
Pale bleached washed-out leaves      → Too much direct light
Dark almost black green leaves       → Not enough light
Wilting despite wet soil             → Root rot or root failure
Sticky coating on leaves             → Pest honeydew — check for aphids or scale
Leaves dropping while still green    → Environmental stress adjustment
Variegation reverting to solid green → Low light — remove all-green shoots
